setupSteps: Check the placard and the pin. Learn which pin or plate slot is the lightest load. Start with the lowest stack or a very light plate load; calves can lift more than you expect, but the first sessions are for learning the stretch and pause.

Set the shoulder-pad height. Step into the machine and adjust (usually a pin or a lever) so the pads rest on the tops of your shoulders with your knees straight but not locked and your heels able to drop below the platform. Too low and you must bend your knees; too high and you cannot stand tall. Machine layouts vary by brand; ask staff if the pad will not adjust.

Foot position. Put the balls of the feet on the platform edge with the heels hanging off. Feet about hip-width apart, toes pointing straight ahead or very slightly out (about 0-15 degrees, est.). Toes in or out may shift work slightly between the two gastrocnemius heads (Riemann 2011 EMG and Nunes 2020 trial as summarised by Biolayne), but the evidence is mixed, so FitPlate keeps the default straight for beginners.
Release and stand. Stand tall, take the weight on your shoulders, release the safety handle or lever if the machine has one, and keep your spine tall with ribs over hips.
Hands. Hold the handles or pad grips lightly, only for balance, with elbows relaxed.
Footwear. Flat, grippy shoes; no bare or socked feet on the platform.

Sit and set the knee pad. Sit upright, put the balls of your feet on the platform, and adjust the knee pad so it rests just above the knees on the lower thighs with no gap (Body-Solid advice: lower the heels fully first, then bring the pad down onto the knees).
Release the safety lever and keep your hips back against the seat; do not lean forward over the pad.
Foot width and toes as for standing (hip-width, toes straight).

steps.title: Set the start position
steps.action: Shoulders under the pads, balls of the feet on the platform, knees straight but soft, heels hanging off, torso tall, hands light on the handles.
steps.feel: Weight on the shoulders and balls of the feet; calves lightly stretched.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ear over shoulder over hip over ankle, knees straight not locked. Front: feet even, toes forward, knees over the second toe.

steps.title: Brace and take a breath
steps.action: Take a small breath in, tighten your stomach lightly, and keep the ribs down.
steps.breathing: In through the nose; do not hold the breath through the rep.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ribs level, no arched lower back.

steps.title: Lower into the stretch
steps.action: Let the heels drop below the platform until you feel a comfortable stretch in the calves.
steps.feel: Long stretch through the calf; no pinch in the front of the ankle or pain at the heel.
steps.visualCheck: Side: heels clearly below the toes; knees still straight; torso still tall.

steps.title: Press up
steps.action: Push through the balls of the big toe and second toe and rise as high as you can on your toes without bending the knees.
steps.visualCheck: Side: heels high, ankles rolling neither in nor out, knees still straight. Front: ankles stay stacked over the feet (no rolling to the outer edge).

steps.title: Hold the top
steps.action: Squeeze and stay on your toes.
steps.visualCheck: Side: highest point of the heel, no forward lean to gain height.

steps.title: Lower under control
steps.action: Slowly lower the heels again to the stretch.
steps.visualCheck: Side: knees stay straight; the weight stack does not bang down.

steps.title: Repeat smoothly for the planned reps with no bouncing
Finish the set. After the last rep, rest the stack (re-engage the safety handle if present), step off the platform one foot at a time, and shake your calves out
steps.visualCheck: Side: the stack is down and the pads have settled before you step out.

commonMistakes.title: Bouncing in the stretch
commonMistakes.text: Bouncing in the stretch. Why: the Achilles tendon returns elastic energy, so the calf does less work and the tendon takes a jolt. Fix: 2 seconds down, 1-2 second pause at the bottom, 1 second up.

commonMistakes.title: Short reps (half range)
commonMistakes.text: Short reps (half range). Why: cuts the stretch, which is the part linked to growth in trials. Fix: heels clearly below the platform, then as high as you can.

commonMistakes.title: Bending the knees to lift more
commonMistakes.text: Bending the knees to lift more. Why: turns it into a squat-like push and removes gastrocnemius stretch. Fix: lower the weight and keep soft straight knees.

commonMistakes.title: Starting too heavy
commonMistakes.text: Starting too heavy. Why: form breaks, ankles roll, and the Achilles tendon is overloaded. Fix: stop at 2-3 reps in reserve until 3 x 12 is smooth.

commonMistakes.title: Rolling onto the outer edge of the foot
commonMistakes.text: Rolling onto the outer edge of the foot. Why: reduces calf work and strains the ankle. Fix: push through the big toe and second toe.

commonMistakes.title: Leaning forward or rocking the hips
commonMistakes.text: Leaning forward or rocking the hips. Why: shifts load to the hips and back. Fix: stand tall, shoulders over hips.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath on every rep
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath on every rep. Why: raises blood pressure (see Safety). Fix: breathe out on the lift.

commonMistakes.title: Dropping the stack
commonMistakes.text: Dropping the stack. Why: loud, jolts the ankle, and can hurt your heel. Fix: control the last 5 cm (2 in, est.).

safetyNotes: Achilles tendon pain or past Achilles injury: NHS physiotherapy leaflets use slow, progressive heel raises as treatment (for example 10-20 reps once or twice a day, each rep about 4-6 seconds), but with a pain rule (some discomfort is acceptable; if pain is worse the next morning, reduce reps or load). Do not start heavy machine work on a painful tendon; get it assessed. If you suddenly cannot rise onto your toes or push your foot down, see a doctor urgently (possible rupture).
Plantar fasciitis or heel pain: the heel raise is used in physiotherapy leaflets for this too, but pain on the underside of the heel when you push up means reduce the load and ask a professional.
Knee problems: the knees stay straight in the standing version, so load on the knee is low; seated machines press a pad on the lower thigh, so stop if the front of the knee hurts.

Balance problems or ankle instability: the standing version needs balance. Use the seated machine, or hold a rail and use the leg press calf press. The seated machine is often described as easier for people with poor balance (fitness retailer sources, not clinical).
Varicose veins, leg swelling or pain in one calf: unexplained calf swelling, warmth or pain needs a doctor's check before exercise (possible clot).

High blood pressure: breath-holding (Valsalva) raises intra-abdominal and blood pressure. A 1995 study found open-glottis breathing safer in heavy lifts; a 2013 review found it raises BP but long-term risks are unconfirmed. Breathe out on each lift; avoid sets to failure.
Pregnancy, recent surgery, osteoporosis: see the table.
